summary:
FLAMEWISE is an interactive website that makes NASA’s research on combustion in microgravity easier to explore. Users choose a material and an environment, adjust gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure and airflow, and compare conditions with Earth.

The website combines an illustrative flame animation with published experiment settings and a research library. An AI assistant explains findings using selected NASA sources and provides links to the original research. We use resources from experiments including BASS-II, Saffire and FLEX.

Our goal is to help students and people interested in space science understand combustion research and its relevance to spacecraft fire safety. The animation is an educational illustration, not a validated fire prediction.
details:
FLAMEWISE is an interactive web application that helps users explore NASA research on combustion in microgravity and its relevance to spacecraft fire safety. We bring an educational flame visualization, published experiment settings and a research assistant into one interface.

Users select acrylic, cotton, SIBAL fabric or a heptane droplet, then adjust gravity, oxygen concentration, airflow and pressure. Environment presets include Earth, the ISS, the Moon and Mars. The Moon and Mars presets represent experiments inside sealed habitats. The Earth comparison keeps the material and atmosphere unchanged while showing the effect of different gravity.

The research library provides access to selected NASA PSI investigation records and NASA NTRS publications. Sources include BASS-II, Saffire and FLEX. Users can load published Saffire test conditions and follow links to the original documents. The AI assistant uses relevant source excerpts and Google Gemini to explain findings with references. Research findings and hypotheses appear separately.

We developed the website using TypeScript, JavaScript, React, HTML and CSS. WebGL and Canvas render the flame animation, Node.js handles server requests, and Vercel hosts the public application. Users need only a web browser, with no special hardware or local AI installation.

Our approach connects questions raised by an interactive experiment with the research behind them. We considered ease of use, access to original sources and scientific limitations. The animation is qualitative and does not reproduce measured flame spread or certify material safety. We aim to help students and people beginning combustion research understand the subject and find relevant evidence more easily.
